inputs.scope: 45s defensive scam awareness Short on work-from-home reshipping jobs

assumptions: Solo/faceless B-roll friendly desk setup; 175-185 WPM brisk narration plus ~2.5s pauses.
Strictly defensive consumer-safety framing; no CTA requested.
limitations: Duration is WPM-estimated (ESTIMATED_WPM), not measured from audio.
Visual brief is CONCEPT_ONLY; no image file generated.
Educational safety awareness only, not individualized legal advice.

evidence.claim: Work-from-home reshipping scams trick job seekers into receiving and forwarding packages purchased with stolen payment methods, leaving victims unpaid and on the shipping trail.
US consumers can report fraudulent job and reshipping offers to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Job seekers who already shared sensitive identity or bank details can follow recovery steps at IdentityTheft.gov.

recommendation.action: Lead directly with a warning against work-from-home parcel relabeling offers, show the home-address liability trail defensively, and end on a 3-step decline/verify/report rule.
recommendation.rationale: Targets the exact job-listing hook victims encounter while keeping content 100% defensive and actionable.

first_frame.concept: 9:16 overhead desk shot of a hand pausing with a blank label over a plain cardboard box beside a generic remote-job card on a laptop.

script.text: If a work-from-home job pays you to inspect and reship packages, stop before you sign anything. The listing looks routine: flexible hours and steady pay for checking boxes delivered to your doorstep. Here's the red flag—legitimate retailers don't run shipping hubs through a stranger's home address. In a reshipping scam, criminals typically buy goods with stolen payment details and ship them to you. You relabel and forward each box, putting your name and home address on the shipping trail while they stay hidden. When payday hits, the paycheck bounces or never arrives—leaving you facing fraud investigators or postal inspectors. Never accept a remote job routing packages through your house, verify employers through their official website, and report suspicious offers to official consumer-protection or postal authorities.
